en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Book of Puzzles,
Chapter on Omniscient Knowledge.
4. The Question on the Nature of Things Regarding Bodhisattvas “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One in the discourse on the nature of things (*dhammatādhamma-pariyāya*):
‘Long ago, for Bodhisattvas, their mother and father were fixed; their enlightenment was fixed; their chief disciples were fixed; their son was fixed.’”
“He becomes one who has a fixed attendant.
Yet again, you say:
“While established in the Tusita realm, the Bodhisatta performs the eight great observations; he observes the time, the continent...”
‘He surveys the time, he surveys the country, he surveys the family, he surveys the mother, he surveys the lifespan, he surveys the month, and he surveys the renunciation.

Venerable Nāgasena, when knowledge is unripened there is no awakening; when knowledge is ripened, it is not possible for even a moment’s delay to occur; a mind that has reached full ripeness cannot be bypassed.
Why does the Bodhisatta examine the time, thinking, “At what time shall I arise”?

When knowledge is unripened, there is no awakening; when knowledge is ripened, it is not possible to delay even for the blink of an eye. Why then does the Bodhisatta examine the clan, thinking, “In what clan shall I arise”?
Venerable Nāgasena, if the parents of the Bodhisatta were already fixed beforehand, then the statement that he “examines the clan” is false.
“If he surveys the family, then the statement that ‘the parents of the Bodhisatta were already predetermined’ is false.
This too is a dilemma from both sides that has come upon you; it must be resolved by you.
“Great King, the parents of the Bodhisatta were indeed predetermined, yet the Bodhisatta also surveys the family.”
But how does one examine the family? One examines the family thus: "Are my mother and father kṣatriyas or brahmins?
In this way, O Great King, one examines the family. Furthermore, eight things must be considered beforehand regarding the future.
Of which eight?
Great King, a merchant must first inspect his merchandise for sale; an elephant-nāga must first look ahead at the path before its trunk reaches it;
and a cart-driver must first look ahead at the ford he has yet to reach.
A navigator must first survey the future shore before setting out the ship;
a physician must first examine the patient’s lifespan before approaching the sick person; one must first ascertain whether a causeway is firm or not before crossing it;
and a monk must first reflect upon the time yet to come before partaking of food.
"One must eat; furthermore, the family of the Bodhisattvas must first be scrutinized as to whether it is a kshatriya family or a brahmin family.
These, O Great King, are the eight things that must be scrutinized beforehand regarding the future."
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
This is the fourth question, on the nature of the Bodhisatta.
